---
title: "Can an LLM read climate policy? An annotation lab"
format: html
---

## The question

> **Do national climate laws and policies commit to concrete, measurable targets, and does this
> differ between countries and regions?**

Answering this properly would mean reading thousands of documents in dozens of languages. Today we ask the question: **if we let a model do the reading,
would we trust the answer?** At each step, notice how the answer to the big question could change
depending on who or what does the coding, which model we use, how we define "target", and what the
model assumes about countries.

::: {.callout-important}
## This is a methods exercise, not a study

We use a dataset that Climate Policy Radar built to train an ML classifier: a few thousand policy
passages labelled by their experts. It is **not** a representative sample of national policies, so
nothing we compute today tells us which countries have targets or how ambitious they are. What it
does give us is expert labels to check ourselves and the models against.
:::

### About the data

- **Source:** [Climate Policy Radar, national-climate-targets](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/national-climate-targets)
  (CC-BY 4.0; Juhasz et al. 2024). 2,610 passages from national climate laws, policies and UNFCCC
  submissions in Climate Policy Radar's database.
- **Labels:** each passage was coded by domain experts as containing a net-zero target, an emissions
  reduction target, another kind of target, or none. A target is "an aim to achieve a specific
  outcome, that is quantifiable and is given a deadline."
- **How passages were chosen:** these passages were chosen to train a model, not to represent countries. Passages likely to
  contain targets were deliberately included, and extra non-target passages were added.
- **Translation:** many passages were machine-translated into English (Google Translate) before
  the experts read them. The `translated` column tells you which.
- **Our sample:** 100 passages, half with a target and half without, chosen by us so the comparison
  is informative.

Work through the sections at your own pace. Run each chunk in order with the green ▶ button, Sections 7 and 8 are optional.

## 0. Setup

This chunk loads the packages and data and defines `ask_model()`, the one function that talks
to the language models. The models run inside Ollama on your own laptop; R sends them a prompt over
a local connection (`localhost`) and gets text back. Nothing leaves your computer.

```{r setup}
library(dplyr)      # data manipulation: filter, mutate, summarise, ...
library(jsonlite)   # reading and writing JSON, the format the models reply in
library(ggplot2)    # plots

# The 100 passages we'll work with today, one row each. Columns: id, text, country, region,
# translated (TRUE if machine-translated into English), expert_target (1 = the experts found a
# target, 0 = not) and expert_type (which kind of target).
passages <- readr::read_csv("data/sample.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Two small open-weights models (about 3 billion parameters each), from Meta and Alibaba.
MODELS <- c("llama3.2:3b", "qwen2.5:3b")

# Send one prompt to a model running in Ollama on this laptop; return its text reply.
#  - format = "json" asks the model to reply in JSON, which is easier to read automatically
#  - temperature = 0 makes it pick its most likely answer instead of sampling, and the fixed
#    seed makes runs as repeatable as possible
ask_model <- function(model, prompt) {
  body <- toJSON(list(model = model, prompt = prompt, stream = FALSE, format = "json",
                      options = list(temperature = 0, seed = 42)), auto_unbox = TRUE)
  h <- curl::new_handle(post = TRUE, postfields = as.character(body), timeout = 120)
  curl::handle_setheaders(h, "Content-Type" = "application/json")
  res <- tryCatch(curl::curl_fetch_memory("http://localhost:11434/api/generate", handle = h),
                  error = \(e) stop("Can't reach Ollama. Open the Ollama app and try again.", call. = FALSE))
  out <- fromJSON(rawToChar(res$content))
  if (!is.null(out$error)) stop(out$error, ". Did you run `ollama pull ", model, "`?", call. = FALSE)
  out$response
}

# Quick check that Ollama is running. You should see a short JSON reply.
ask_model(MODELS[1], 'Reply with the JSON {"ok": 1}')
```

## 1. The coding scheme

This is the definition the experts used. The models get exactly this text.

`make_prompt()` wraps each passage in the same instructions, and `read_label()` pulls the 0 or 1
out of the model's reply. Small models don't always follow instructions, so if the reply has no
usable answer we record `NA` (missing) rather than guessing.

```{r codebook}
# The coding scheme, in words. This text is the only thing that tells the model what a "target" is.
DEFINITION <- "A TARGET is an aim to achieve a specific outcome that is quantifiable and has a
deadline. Examples: cut emissions 40% by 2030; 50% renewable electricity by 2035; net zero by 2050.
A general aim without a number or a date is NOT a target."

# Build the full prompt for one passage: role, definition, question, required answer format, passage.
make_prompt <- function(text, definition = DEFINITION) {
  paste0("You are coding passages from national climate laws and policies.\n\n",
         definition, "\n\n",
         "Does the passage below contain a target? Respond with JSON only: ",
         '{"target": 1} or {"target": 0}.\n\nPassage:\n', text)
}

# Pull the 0/1 out of the model's reply (NA if it didn't follow instructions).
# The pattern looks for "target", a colon, optional spaces and quotes, then a 0 or 1.
read_label <- function(reply) {
  x <- regmatches(reply, regexpr('"target"\\s*:\\s*"?[01]', reply))
  if (length(x) == 0) NA_integer_ else as.integer(substring(x, nchar(x)))
}
```

## 2. Code 10 passages yourself

Read each passage and decide: target (1) or no target (0)? Don't look anything up.

```{r show-passages}
#| results: asis
# Print the first 10 passages. (results: asis lets the bold numbering show as formatting.)
for (i in 1:10) cat("**", i, ".** ", passages$text[i], "\n\n", sep = "")
```

Type your answers, in order, then run the chunk.

```{r my-labels}
my_labels <- c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA)   # replace each NA with 1 or 0
```

## 3. Run the two models

This sends every passage to each model, one at a time, and collects the answers. It takes a few
minutes. If you change the definition or prompt in section 1, rerun this chunk to see the effect.

```{r run-models}
# Ask each model about each passage. sapply() loops over the passages and collects one
# 0/1/NA per passage.
model_labels <- passages |> select(id)
for (m in MODELS) {
  message("Running ", m, " ...")
  model_labels[[m]] <- sapply(passages$text, \(t) read_label(ask_model(m, make_prompt(t))))
}

# Put the passages, expert labels and model labels side by side in one table.
results <- passages |> left_join(model_labels, by = "id")
```

## 4. How well do they agree?

Percentage agreement flatters: if most passages had no target, saying "no" every time would score
well. **Cohen's kappa** corrects for agreement you would get by chance (0 = chance, 1 = perfect).

```{r agreement}
# Cohen's kappa for two coders who each gave 0/1 labels to the same passages.
kappa <- function(a, b) {
  # Only compare passages where both coders gave an answer
  ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b); a <- a[ok]; b <- b[ok]
  # How often they actually agree
  p_observed <- mean(a == b)
  # How often they would agree by chance, given how often each says 1:
  # both say 1 by chance, plus both say 0 by chance
  p_chance <- mean(a) * mean(b) + (1 - mean(a)) * (1 - mean(b))
  # Agreement beyond chance, scaled so that 1 = perfect and 0 = no better than chance
  (p_observed - p_chance) / (1 - p_chance)
}

# Everyone we want to compare: the experts, you, and the two models.
# The names are what's printed; the values are the column names in `results`.
coders <- c("Experts" = "expert_target", "You (first 10)" = "me", setNames(MODELS, MODELS))
# Your labels cover only the first 10 passages; the rest are NA.
results$me <- c(my_labels, rep(NA, nrow(results) - 10))

# One row per coder:
#  - passages: how many passages they labelled
#  - targets_found: how many they said contain a target
#  - agree_with_experts: share of passages where they gave the same label as the experts
#  - kappa_vs_experts: agreement beyond chance
tibble(
  coder = names(coders),
  passages = sapply(coders, \(c) sum(!is.na(results[[c]]))),
  targets_found = sapply(coders, \(c) sum(results[[c]], na.rm = TRUE)),
  agree_with_experts = sapply(coders, \(c) mean(results[[c]] == results$expert_target, na.rm = TRUE)),
  kappa_vs_experts = sapply(coders, \(c) kappa(results[[c]], results$expert_target))
) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r models-vs-each-other}
# Do the two models agree with each other? (Two models can agree well and both be wrong.)
round(kappa(results[[MODELS[1]]], results[[MODELS[2]]]), 2)

# Where does the first model go wrong? Rows = experts, columns = model.
# Top-right cell: the model found a target the experts didn't (false positive).
# Bottom-left cell: the model missed a target the experts found (false negative).
table(experts = results$expert_target, model = results[[MODELS[1]]], useNA = "ifany")
```

**Discuss:** Did you beat the models? Do the models make the same kind of mistake (missing targets,
or seeing targets that aren't there)? **Back to the big question:** look at `targets_found`. If
each model read every national policy, would they give the same answer about how many countries
have concrete targets?

## 5. Read the disagreements

Here are the 10 passages you coded, with your label, the experts' label and both models' labels
side by side. Passages where anyone disagrees with the experts are marked ⚠️.

```{r disagreements}
#| results: asis
# The 10 passages you coded (your labels are in the `me` column, from section 4).
first10 <- results |> slice(1:10)

# Show a label, or "no answer" if it's missing
show <- \(x) if (is.na(x)) "no answer" else x

for (i in seq_len(nrow(first10))) {
  d <- first10[i, ]
  # Does anyone (you or either model) disagree with the experts on this passage?
  labels <- c(d$me, d[[MODELS[1]]], d[[MODELS[2]]])
  flag <- if (any(labels != d$expert_target, na.rm = TRUE)) "⚠️ " else ""
  cat(flag, "**Passage ", d$id, "** (", d$country, if (d$translated) ", machine-translated", ")  \n",
      "Experts: ", d$expert_target, " (", d$expert_type, ") · You: ", show(d$me), " · ",
      MODELS[1], ": ", show(d[[MODELS[1]]]), " · ", MODELS[2], ": ", show(d[[MODELS[2]]]), "\n\n",
      "> ", d$text, "\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

For each ⚠️ passage, decide: **a coding error** (yours or a model's), **an unclear definition**, or
**the experts got it wrong**? Keep a tally with your partner. How many "errors" are really the
model's fault? Are the errors
spread evenly, or concentrated in translated passages?

## 6. ✏️ Change the prompt

Rewrite the definition below. Try loosening it (drop "quantifiable"?), tightening it, or adding an
example. Then see how many labels change.

```{r new-prompt}
# ✏️ Edit this definition. Everything else in the prompt stays the same.
MY_DEFINITION <- "A TARGET is any climate or energy goal the government commits to."

# Ask the first model again about every passage, using your definition (about 1 minute).
new_labels <- sapply(passages$text, \(t) read_label(ask_model(MODELS[1], make_prompt(t, MY_DEFINITION))))

# Compare with the first model's answers under the original definition.
cat("Labels that changed:", sum(new_labels != results[[MODELS[1]]], na.rm = TRUE), "of", nrow(passages), "\n")
cat("Targets found, original prompt:", sum(results[[MODELS[1]]], na.rm = TRUE),
    "  your prompt:", sum(new_labels, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Kappa vs experts, original prompt:", round(kappa(results[[MODELS[1]]], results$expert_target), 2), "\n")
cat("Kappa vs experts, your prompt:    ", round(kappa(new_labels, results$expert_target), 2), "\n")
```

**Discuss:** Did you change the *wording* or the *thing being measured*? If a researcher tried ten
prompts and reported the best one, what would that do to their findings? **Back to the big
question:** a government that writes "we aim to decarbonise" has a target under your definition but
not under the experts'. Whose definition should a study of national commitments use?

## 7. Bonus: same text, different country

One passage, identical wording; only the country name changes. Any difference comes from the model,
not the text.

```{r country-swap}
# Take the first passage the experts marked as containing a target.
passage <- results$text[results$expert_target == 1][1]
# The countries we'll attribute it to, one at a time.
countries <- c("Switzerland", "Brazil", "India", "Nigeria", "Indonesia", "United States")

# Ask how likely `country` is to achieve what the passage describes, on a 1-5 scale.
# Returns NA if the reply isn't a usable number. Same prompt as country_swap_batch.R.
swap_score <- function(text, country, model = MODELS[1]) {
  p <- paste0("This passage is from a climate policy published by the government of ", country,
              ":\n\n", text, "\n\nHow likely is it that ", country,
              " will achieve this on time? Respond with JSON only: {\"score\": 1 to 5}")
  s <- tryCatch(as.numeric(fromJSON(ask_model(model, p))$score), error = \(e) NA_real_)
  if (length(s) != 1 || is.na(s) || s < 1 || s > 5) NA_real_ else s
}
# Same passage, six country names, six scores.
tibble(country = countries, likelihood_1_to_5 = sapply(countries, \(c) swap_score(passage, c)))
```

One passage tells us little. Does the pattern hold across many passages? If someone has already run
`country_swap_batch.R` (every suitable target passage, about 300, times six countries), this chunk
loads those results. Otherwise it runs a small batch of 20 passages here (120 calls, a few minutes).

```{r country-swap-scale}
# Load the batch results if they exist; otherwise score 20 random passages x 6 countries here.
if (file.exists("data/country_swap_results.csv")) {
  swaps <- readr::read_csv("data/country_swap_results.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  pool <- readr::read_csv("data/target_pool.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> slice_sample(n = 20)
  swaps <- expand.grid(id = pool$id, country = countries, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
    left_join(select(pool, id, text), by = "id")
  swaps$score <- mapply(swap_score, swaps$text, swaps$country)
}
cat("Passages:", n_distinct(swaps$id), "\n")
# swaps now has one row per passage x country, with the model's score in `score`.

# Compare each score with the average for the same passage, so only the country name differs.
# Example: if a passage gets 4 for Switzerland and its average across countries is 3, Switzerland's
# shift for that passage is +1. Averaging shifts across passages gives each country's overall shift.
# se is the standard error; low and high give a 95% confidence interval.
by_country <- swaps |>
  group_by(id) |> mutate(shift = score - mean(score, na.rm = TRUE)) |> ungroup() |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(score)), mean_score = mean(score, na.rm = TRUE),
            se = sd(shift, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), shift = mean(shift, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(low = shift - 1.96 * se, high = shift + 1.96 * se) |>
  arrange(shift)
by_country |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# For how many passages does the score change at all when only the country name changes?
varies <- swaps |> group_by(id) |> summarise(v = n_distinct(na.omit(score)) > 1)
cat("Share of passages where the score changes with the country name:", round(mean(varies$v), 2), "\n")
```

```{r country-swap-plot}
#| fig-height: 4
# Dot = average shift for each country; bars = 95% confidence interval; dashed line = no shift.
# Countries to the right were scored as more likely to succeed than the same text elsewhere.
ggplot(by_country, aes(x = shift, y = reorder(country, shift))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Score relative to the same passage's average (95% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Discuss:** There is no right answer to "how likely is this to be achieved", so this measures the
model's assumptions, not the countries. **Back to the big question:** if a study used an LLM to
judge how *credible* or *ambitious* each country's targets are, could regional differences in its
results come from the model rather than the policies? Would a small validation sample catch that?

## 8. If you have time: ask your own question

So far the experts wrote the codebook. Now you do. Pick a yes/no question about climate policy
text, write a definition, and test a model on 30 new passages from the Climate Policy Radar data.
There are **no expert labels** for your question: your own hand-coding is the benchmark.

Some ideas:
- Does the passage mention **adaptation**, not only emissions cuts?
- Does it mention **Indigenous peoples or local communities**?
- Does it set a goal for **nature** (the worked example below)?
- Does it place responsibility on a **specific actor** (a ministry, industry, cities)?

```{r own-question-setup}
# 30 passages you haven't seen yet. These have no expert labels.
more <- readr::read_csv("data/more_passages.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> head(30)

# ✏️ Replace the question and definition with your own (or keep this worked example).

MY_QUESTION   <- "Does this passage include a goal or measure for nature?"
MY_DEFINITION <- "A passage is about NATURE if it sets a goal or describes a measure for forests,
land use, ecosystems, protected areas or biodiversity. Measures that only mention energy, transport,
industry or buildings do not count."

# Same idea as make_prompt() and read_label() above, but for your yes/no question.
ask_yes_no <- function(text, model = MODELS[1]) {
  prompt <- paste0("You are coding passages from national climate laws and policies.\n\n",
                   MY_DEFINITION, "\n\nQuestion: ", MY_QUESTION, "\n",
                   'Respond with JSON only: {"answer": 1} for yes or {"answer": 0} for no.',
                   "\n\nPassage:\n", text)
  reply <- ask_model(model, prompt)
  x <- regmatches(reply, regexpr('"answer"\\s*:\\s*"?[01]', reply))
  if (length(x) == 0) NA_integer_ else as.integer(substring(x, nchar(x)))
}
```

First, code the first 10 passages yourself, using your own definition.

```{r own-question-passages}
#| results: asis
# Print the first 10 of the new passages for you to code.
for (i in 1:10) cat("**", i, ".** ", more$text[i], "\n\n", sep = "")
```

```{r own-question-labels}
my_answers <- c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA)   # 1 = yes, 0 = no
```

Now let the model answer all 30 passages (about 1 minute).

```{r own-question-run}
# Ask the model your question about all 30 passages.
more$model_answer <- sapply(more$text, ask_yes_no)

# On the 10 you coded, how well does the model agree with you?

cat("Model vs you, first 10 passages: kappa =",
    round(kappa(more$model_answer[1:10], my_answers), 2), "\n")
cat("Model said yes to", sum(more$model_answer, na.rm = TRUE), "of", nrow(more), "passages\n\n")
```

Read what the model said yes to on the 20 passages you didn't code. Do you agree?

```{r own-question-check}
#| results: asis
# Print the passages (among the 20 you didn't code) where the model answered yes.
yes <- more |> slice(11:30) |> filter(model_answer == 1)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(yes))) cat("**", yes$country[i], "** ", yes$text[i], "\n\n", sep = "")
```

**Discuss:** How hard was it to write a definition you could apply consistently? Would a
classmate code your 10 passages the same way? Is a 10-passage benchmark enough, and where does
your question sit on the risk ladder?

## 9. From this sample to a whole corpus

Suppose a model performed well on everything above. Climate Policy Radar also publishes the
[full text of its database](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ClimatePolicyRadar/all-document-text-data):
tens of millions of text passages from national climate laws, policies and UNFCCC submissions.

If you want to look at it, the bonus notebook `bonus_cloud_native.qmd` queries the whole corpus in
place, without downloading it, and draws a random sample of passages the experts never labelled.

   finance?).

   Before trusting results across the corpus, what else would you need? Think about which
